chapter: Billy Hicks, the Apollo and Roy Eldridge
title: Roy defends him against manager Joe Glaser, who wanted Sid Catlett
summary: At the Arcadia, a $50-a-week job, Roy stood up for his young drummer; Roy and Clyde Hart pushed him to learn to read.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Well, while we're at rehearsal, Joe Glazier, who was Roy's manager, comes in and saw me sitting up there and he said, "Where's Sid Catlett?" So Roy said "Well, this is my drummer here." And that's one reason why I have a lot of respect and a warm spot in my heart for Roy, because he stood up for me with Joe Glazier. When Joe Glazier said, "Well, look, I want Big Sid in this band."
He wanted Big Sid in the band, huh?
Yeah, he wanted Sid Catlett in the band, because you know, at the Arcadia, that was one of the best jobs in New York at that time. The job paid $50 a week.
And they only took out 50¢ for Social Security, because Social Security had just started them. I mean, it hadn't been around but two years.
And I only had to pay 50¢ out of my $50, so I got $49.50. One of the best jobs in New York!

So Roy takes his horn and puts it on the stand, and says to Joe Glazier, "Well, I tell you what you do -- you play this God damned trumpet, then, if you want to run my band" -- and he left and went upstairs.
And that's how I stayed there with Roy. But if it was left up to Joe Glazier, Sid Catlett would have been in
that band instead of me. So, Roy is the one responsible for me learning how to read, because him and Clyde Hart, Park, they used to play checkers in between sets.
